idiom_name: Func<T,TResult> delegates plus a Compose extension method
implementation_notes: Delegates make methods values - `Func<string, string> normalize = s => s.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();` - and extension methods add the missing combinator without deriving from or modifying any type (learn.microsoft.com), so composition is one generic extension: `public static Func<A, C> Compose<A, B, C>(this Func<A, B> f, Func<B, C> g) => x => g(f(x));`. The BCL ships no Compose; its compositional surface is LINQ, where Select/Where/Aggregate chain transformations over sequences. The hand-written extension or a nested lambda replaces the classic structure, and it earns its place when the chain is a named value shared across handlers; for a one-off transformation the inline composed lambda is clearer.
pitfalls: Every Func invocation is a delegate call: anonymous chains are not inlined and capture allocations are created once per composition, which matters inside per-item loops.
Composing a null delegate only fails at call time; the BCL's own combinators validate arguments eagerly, so validate steps when a chain is assembled from configuration.
Method-group conversions allocate a fresh delegate instance each time, so hoist the composed delegate into a static readonly field when the chain is built in a hot path.
